title: What if you slept like a dolphin, half your brain at a time?

narration.heading: Half asleep
narration.text: You lie down to sleep, but only half of your brain switches off.

narration.heading: Dolphins
narration.text: Dolphins live like this. They're voluntary breathers, so they have to choose to surface for every breath.

narration.heading: Half and half
narration.text: So while they sleep, one half of the brain rests and the other half stays awake.

narration.heading: Naps at sea
narration.text: They sleep about eight hours a day, in short stretches, swimming slowly near the surface.

narration.heading: One eye open
narration.text: Some birds do it too. Their open eye is wired to the half of the brain that's awake.

narration.heading: On guard
narration.text: It helps them spot danger. Birds sleep this way more when predators are about.

narration.heading: Sky naps
narration.text: Frigatebirds even sleep while flying, mostly as they circle on rising air.

narration.heading: The twist
narration.text: The twist? You do a little of this too. Your first night somewhere new, part of your left brain stays more alert.

narration.heading: Your call
narration.text: Odd beeps in your right ear wake you faster that night. Would you want dolphin sleep every night?

hook.banner: What if half your brain slept?

skit.text: Half my brain asleep? That explains my last update.

titles: What if you slept like a dolphin, half your brain at a time?
Dolphins sleep with half their brain, and so do you, sometimes
youtube.description: How dolphins and some birds sleep with one half of the brain while the other half keeps watch, and the night your own brain does something similar.

sources.claim: Bottlenose dolphins are voluntary breathers who must deliberately surface to breathe; while they sleep one brain hemisphere stays active while the other shuts down; they sleep about 8 hours a day in short increments, swimming slowly near the surface

In birds sleeping with one hemisphere, the open eye is on the opposite side to the awake hemisphere; birds use it more as predation risk rises; frigatebirds sleep mostly while circling air currents in flight

On the first night in a new place, a network in the left hemisphere stayed more active during deep sleep, and irregular beeps in the right ear led to faster waking (Tamaki et al., Current Biology 2016)
